breaths.text: And made it thicker; while the phantom king Sent out at times a voice; and here or there
Slew on and burnt, crying, “No king of ours, No son of Uther, and no king of ours;”
Descended, and the solid earth became As nothing, but the King stood out in heaven,
Ulfius, and Brastias and Bedivere, Back to the court of Arthur answering yea.
And honoured most, Sir Lancelot, to ride forth And bring the Queen;—and watched him from the gates:
(For then was latter April) and returned Among the flowers, in May, with Guinevere.
Chief of the church in Britain, and before The stateliest of her altar-shrines, the King
The fair beginners of a nobler time, And glorying in their vows and him, his knights
Far shone the fields of May through open door, The sacred altar blossomed white with May,
They gazed on all earth’s beauty in their Queen, Rolled incense, and there past along the hymns
Sware at the shrine of Christ a deathless love: And Arthur said, “Behold, thy doom is mine.
To whom the Queen replied with drooping eyes, “King and my lord, I love thee to the death!”
“Reign ye, and live and love, and make the world Other, and may thy Queen be one with thee,
Fulfil the boundless purpose of their King!”
Great Lords from Rome before the portal stood, In scornful stillness gazing as they past;
With sun and cloth of gold, the trumpets blew, And Arthur’s knighthood sang before the King:—
“Blow, trumpet, for the world is white with May;
Blow through the living world—‘Let the King reign.’
“Shall Rome or Heathen rule in Arthur’s realm?
Fall battleaxe, and flash brand! Let the King reign.
“Strike for the King and live! his knights have heard
Fall battleaxe, and flash brand! Let the King reign.
“Blow trumpet! he will lift us from the dust.
Clang battleaxe, and clash brand! Let the King reign.
“Strike for the King and die! and if thou diest,
Clang battleaxe, and clash brand! Let the King reign.
“Blow, for our Sun is mighty in his May!
Clang battleaxe, and clash brand! Let the King reign.
“The King will follow Christ, and we the King
Fall battleaxe, and flash brand! Let the King reign.”
There at the banquet those great Lords from Rome, The slowly-fading mistress of the world,
But Arthur spake, “Behold, for these have sworn To wage my wars, and worship me their King;
And we that fight for our fair father Christ, Seeing that ye be grown too weak and old
No tribute will we pay:” so those great lords Drew back in wrath, and Arthur strove with Rome.
Were all one will, and through that strength the King Drew in the petty princedoms under him,
The heathen hordes, and made a realm and reigned.
And tallest, Gareth, in a showerful spring Stared at the spate. A slender-shafted Pine
“How he went down,” said Gareth, “as a false knight Or evil king before my lance if lance
Bearing all down in thy precipitancy— And yet thou art but swollen with cold snows
The Maker’s, and not knowest, and I that know, Have strength and wit, in my good mother’s hall
Prisoned, and kept and coaxed and whistled to— Since the good mother holds me still a child!
A worse were better; yet no worse would I. Heaven yield her for it, but in me put force
Until she let me fly discaged to sweep In ever-highering eagle-circles up
Down upon all things base, and dash them dead, A knight of Arthur, working out his will,
With Modred hither in the summertime, Asked me to tilt with him, the proven knight.
Then I so shook him in the saddle, he said, ‘Thou hast half prevailed against me,’ said so—he—
For he is alway sullen: what care I?”

Asked, “Mother, though ye count me still the child, Sweet mother, do ye love the child?” She laughed, “Thou art but a wild-goose to question it.” “Then, mother, an ye love the child,” he said, “Being a goose and rather tame than wild,
An ’twere but of the goose and golden eggs.”
“Nay, nay, good mother, but this egg of mine Was finer gold than any goose can lay;
Almost beyond eye-reach, on such a palm As glitters gilded in thy Book of Hours.
A lusty youth, but poor, who often saw The splendour sparkling from aloft, and thought ‘An I could climb and lay my hand upon it,
But ever when he reached a hand to climb, One, that had loved him from his childhood, caught And stayed him, ‘Climb not lest thou break thy neck,
Sweet mother, neither clomb, nor brake his neck, But brake his very heart in pining for it,
To whom the mother said, “True love, sweet son, had risked himself and climbed,
And Gareth answered her with kindling eyes, “Gold?” said I gold?—ay then, why he, or she,
Had ventured—had the thing I spake of been Mere gold—but this was all of that true steel,
And lightnings played about it in the storm, And all the little fowl were flurried at it,
That sent him from his senses: let me go.”
“Hast thou no pity upon my loneliness? Lo, where thy father Lot beside the hearth
For ever since when traitor to the King He fought against him in the Barons’ war,
His age hath slowly droopt, and now lies there A yet-warm corpse, and yet unburiable, No more; nor sees, nor hears, nor speaks, nor knows.
Albeit neither loved with that full love I feel for thee, nor worthy such a love:
And thee, mine innocent, the jousts, the wars, Who never knewest finger-ache, nor pang
In those brain-stunning shocks, and tourney-falls, Frights to my heart; but stay: follow the deer
So make thy manhood mightier day by day; Sweet is the chase: and I will seek thee out
Thy climbing life, and cherish my prone year, Till falling into Lot’s forgetfulness
Stay, my best son! ye are yet more boy than man.”
Hear yet once more the story of the child. For, mother, there was once a King, like ours.
Asked for a bride; and thereupon the King Set two before him. One was fair, strong, armed—
Desired her; one good lack, no man desired. And these were the conditions of the King:
Must wed that other, whom no man desired, A red-faced bride who knew herself so vile,
Nor fronted man or woman, eye to eye— Yea—some she cleaved to, but they died of her.
How can ye keep me tethered to you—Shame. Man am I grown, a man’s work must I do.
Live pure, speak true, right wrong, follow the King— Else, wherefore born?”
“Sweet son, for there be many who deem him not, Or will not deem him, wholly proven King—
When I was frequent with him in my youth, And heard him Kingly speak, and doubted him
Of closest kin to me: yet—wilt thou leave Thine easeful biding here, and risk thine all,
Stay, till the cloud that settles round his birth Hath lifted but a little. Stay, sweet son.”
So that ye yield me—I will walk through fire, Mother, to gain it—your full leave to go.
From off the threshold of the realm, and crushed The Idolaters, and made the people free?
So when the Queen, who long had sought in vain
Found her son’s will unwaveringly one, She answered craftily, “Will ye walk through fire? Who walks through fire will hardly heed the smoke.
Before thou ask the King to make thee knight, Of thine obedience and thy love to me,
And Gareth cried, “A hard one, or a hundred, so I go.
But slowly spake the mother looking at him, “Prince, thou shalt go disguised to Arthur’s hall,
Among the scullions and the kitchen-knaves, And those that hand the dish across the bar.
And thou shalt serve a twelvemonth and a day.”
Beheld his only way to glory lead Low down through villain kitchen-vassalage,
To pass thereby; so should he rest with her, Closed in her castle from the sound of arms.
“The thrall in person may be free in soul, And I shall see the jousts. Thy son am I,
I therefore yield me freely to thy will; For hence will I, disguised, and hire myself
Nor tell my name to any—no, not the King.”
Full of the wistful fear that he would go, And turning toward him wheresoe’er he turned,
When wakened by the wind which with full voice Swept bellowing through the darkness on to dawn,
That still had tended on him from his birth, Before the wakeful mother heard him, went.
Southward they set their faces. The birds made Melody on branch, and melody in mid air.
And the live green had kindled into flowers, For it was past the time of Easterday.
That broadened toward the base of Camelot, Far off they saw the silver-misty morn
That rose between the forest and the field. At times the summit of the high city flashed;
Pricked through the mist; at times the great gate shone Only, that opened on the field below:
Then those who went with Gareth were amazed,
Here is a city of Enchanters, built By fairy Kings.” The second echoed him, “Lord, we have heard from our wise man at home
But only changeling out of Fairyland, Who drave the heathen hence by sorcery
“Lord, there is no such city anywhere, But all a vision.”
With laughter, swearing he had glamour enow In his own blood, his princedom, youth and hopes,
So pushed them all unwilling toward the gate. And there was no gate like it under heaven.
And rippled like an ever-fleeting wave, The Lady of the Lake stood: all her dress
But like the cross her great and goodly arms Stretched under the cornice and upheld:
And down from one a sword was hung, from one A censer, either worn with wind and storm;
And in the space to left of her, and right, Were Arthur’s wars in weird devices done,
Were nothing, so inveterately, that men Were giddy gazing there; and over all High on the top were those three Queens, the friends
Then those with Gareth for so long a space
The dragon-boughts and elvish emblemings Began to move, seethe, twine and curl: they called
And Gareth likewise on them fixt his eyes
Out of the city a blast of music pealed. Back from the gate started the three, to whom
Long-bearded, saying, “Who be ye, my sons?”
Who leaving share in furrow come to see The glories of our King: but these, my men, (Your city moved so weirdly in the mist)
From Fairyland; and whether this be built By magic, and by fairy Kings and Queens;
Or all a vision: and this music now Hath scared them both, but tell thou these the truth.”
And saying, “Son, I have seen the good ship sail Keel upward, and mast downward, in the heavens,
And here is truth; but an it please thee not, Take thou the truth as thou hast told it me.
And Fairy Queens have built the city, son; They came from out a sacred mountain-cleft
And built it to the music of their harps. And, as thou sayest, it is enchanted, son,
Saving the King; though some there be that hold The King a shadow, and the city real:
Beneath this archway, then wilt thou become A thrall to his enchantments, for the King
A man should not be bound by, yet the which No man can keep; but, so thou dread to swear,
Without, among the cattle of the field. For an ye heard a music, like enow
To music, therefore never built at all, And therefore built for ever.”
Angered, “Old master, reverence thine own beard That looks as white as utter truth, and seems
Why mockest thou the stranger that hath been To thee fair-spoken?”
“Know ye not then the Riddling of the Bards? ‘Confusion, and illusion, and relation,
I mock thee not but as thou mockest me, And all that see thee, for thou art not who
And now thou goest up to mock the King, Who cannot brook the shadow of any lie.”
Turned to the right, and past along the plain; Whom Gareth looking after said, “My men,
Here on the threshold of our enterprise. Let love be blamed for it, not she, nor I:
With all good cheer
Camelot, a city of shadowy palaces And stately, rich in emblem and the work
Which Merlin’s hand, the Mage at Arthur’s court, Knowing all arts, had touched, and everywhere
And pinnacle, and had made it spire to heaven. And ever and anon a knight would pass
Clashed; and the sound was good to Gareth’s ear. And out of bower and casement shyly glanced
And all about a healthful people stept As in the presence of a gracious king.
A voice, the voice of Arthur, and beheld Far over heads in that long-vaulted hall
Throned, and delivering doom—and looked no more— But felt his young heart hammering in his ears,
The truthful King will doom me when I speak.” Yet pressing on, though all in fear to find
Nor other, but in all the listening eyes Of those tall knights, that ranged about the throne,
Of dawn, and faith in their great King, with pure Affection, and the light of victory,
Then came a widow crying to the King, “A boon, Sir King! Thy father, Uther, reft
For howsoe’er at first he proffered gold, Yet, for the field was pleasant in our eyes,
Perforce, and left us neither gold nor field.”
To whom the woman weeping, “Nay, my lord, The field was pleasant in my husband’s eye.”
And thrice the gold for Uther’s use thereof, According to the years. No boon is here,
Accursed, who from the wrongs his father did Would shape himself a right!”
Came yet another widow crying to him, “A boon, Sir King! Thine enemy, King, am I.
A knight of Uther in the Barons’ war, When Lot and many another rose and fought
I held with these, and loathe to ask thee aught. Yet lo! my husband’s brother had my son Thralled in his castle, and hath starved him dead;
Which thou that slewest the sire hast left the son. So though I scarce can ask it thee for hate,
Kill the foul thief, and wreak me for my son.”
“A boon, Sir King! I am her kinsman, I. Give me to right her wrong, and slay the man.”
“A boon, Sir King! even that thou grant her none, This railer, that hath mocked thee in full hall—
But Arthur, “We sit King, to help the wronged
Peace to thee, woman, with thy loves and hates! The kings of old had doomed thee to the flames,
And Uther slit thy tongue: but get thee hence— Lest that rough humour of the kings of old
Go likewise; lay him low and slay him not, But bring him here, that I may judge the right,
Then, be he guilty, by that deathless King Who lived and died for men, the man shall die.”
A name of evil savour in the land, The Cornish king. In either hand he bore
A field of charlock in the sudden sun Between two showers, a cloth of palest gold,
Delivering, that his lord, the vassal king, Was even upon his way to Camelot;
Had made his goodly cousin, Tristram, knight, And, for himself was of the greater state,
Would yield him this large honour all the more; So prayed him well to accept this cloth of gold,
Then Arthur cried to rend the cloth, to rend
An oak-tree smouldered there. “The goodly knight! What! shall the shield of Mark stand among these?”
A stately pile,—whereof along the front, Some blazoned, some but carven, and some blank,
Rose, and high-arching overbrowed the hearth. And under every shield a knight was named:
When some good knight had done one noble deed, His arms were carven only; but if twain
The shield was blank and bare without a sign Saving the name beneath; and Gareth saw
And Modred’s blank as death; and Arthur cried To rend the cloth and cast it on the hearth.
“More like are we to reave him of his crown
The kings we found, ye know we stayed their hands From war among themselves, but left them kings;
Truth-speaking, brave, good livers, them we enrolled Among us, and they sit within our hall. But as Mark hath tarnished the great name of king,
And, seeing he hath sent us cloth of gold, Return, and meet, and hold him from our eyes,
Silenced for ever—craven—a man of plots, Craft, poisonous counsels, wayside ambushings—
Look to thy wants, and send thee satisfied— Accursed, who strikes nor lets the hand be seen!”
With noise of ravage wrought by beast and man, And evermore a knight would ride away.
Down on the shoulders of the twain, his men, Approached between them toward the King, and asked, “A boon, Sir King (his voice was all ashamed),
I seem—leaning on these? grant me to serve For meat and drink among thy kitchen-knaves
Hereafter I will fight.”
“A goodly youth and worth a goodlier boon! But so thou wilt no goodlier, then must Kay,
He rose and past; then Kay, a man of mien
Root-bitten by white lichen,
“Lo ye now!
God wot, he had not beef and brewis enow, However that might chance! but an he work,
And sleeker shall he shine than any hog.”
Sleuth-hound thou knowest, and gray, and all the hounds; A horse thou knowest, a man thou dost not know:
High nose, a nostril large and fine, and hands Large, fair and fine!—Some young lad’s mystery—
Is noble-natured. Treat him with all grace, Lest he should come to shame thy judging of him.”
Think ye this fellow will poison the King’s dish? Nay, for he spake too fool-like: mystery!
For horse and armour: fair and fine, forsooth! Sir Fine-face, Sir Fair-hands? but see thou to it
Undo thee not—and leave my man to me.”
The sooty yoke of kitchen-vassalage; Ate with young lads his portion by the door,

Nor any cry of Christian heard thereon, Nor yet of heathen; only the wan wave
Swaying the helpless hands, and up and down Tumbling the hollow helmets of the fallen, And shivered brands that once had fought with Rome,
The voice of days of old and days to be.
And whiter than the mist that all day long Had held the field of battle was the King:
“Hearest thou this great voice that shakes the world,
And beats upon the faces of the dead, My dead, as though they had not died for me?—
Confusion, till I know not what I am, Nor whence I am, nor whether I be King.
Then spake the bold Sir Bedivere: “My King,
There also will I worship thee as King. Yet still thy life is whole, and still I live Who love thee; but who hates thee, he that brought
Modred, unharmed, the traitor of thine house.”
Then spake the King: “My house hath been my doom.
Who hath but dwelt beneath one roof with me. My house are rather they who sware my vows,
And well for thee, saying in my dark hour, When all the purport of my throne hath failed,
King am I, whatsoever be their cry; And one last act of kinghood shalt thou see
Made at the man: then Modred smote his liege Hard on that helm which many a heathen sword
Striking the last stroke with Excalibur, Slew him, and all but slain himself, he fell.
Among the mountains by the winter sea; Until King Arthur’s Table, man by man,
King Arthur. Then, because his wound was deep, The bold Sir Bedivere uplifted him,
A broken chancel with a broken cross, That stood on a dark strait of barren land:
Lay a great water, and the moon was full.
“The sequel of today unsolders all The goodliest fellowship of famous knights
They sleep—the men I loved. I think that we Shall never more, at any future time,
Walking about the gardens and the halls Of Camelot, as in the days that were.
Though Merlin sware that I should come again To rule once more; but, let what will be, be,
That without help I cannot last till morn. Thou therefore take my brand Excalibur,
In those old days, one summer noon, an arm Rose up from out the bosom of the lake,
Holding the sword—and how I rowed across And took it, and have worn it, like a king;
In aftertime, this also shall be known: But now delay not: take Excalibur,
Watch what thou seest, and lightly bring me word.”
“It is not meet, Sir King, to leave thee thus, Aidless, alone, and smitten through the helm—
Yet I thy hest will all perform at full, Watch what I see, and lightly bring thee word.”
And in the moon athwart the place of tombs, Where lay the mighty bones of ancient men,
Shrill, chill, with flakes of foam. He, stepping down By zigzag paths, and juts of pointed rock,
There drew he forth the brand Excalibur,
Brightening the skirts of a long cloud, ran forth And sparkled keen with frost against the hilt:
Myriads of topaz-lights, and jacinth-work Of subtlest jewellery. He gazed so long
This way and that dividing the swift mind, In act to throw: but at the last it seemed
There in the many-knotted waterflags, That whistled stiff and dry about the marge.
Then spake King Arthur to Sir Bedivere: “Hast thou performed my mission which I gave?
And answer made the bold Sir Bedivere: “I heard the ripple washing in the reeds,
To whom replied King Arthur, faint and pale: “Thou hast betrayed thy nature and thy name,
Thy fealty, nor like a noble knight: For surer sign had followed, either hand,
This is a shameful thing for men to lie. Yet now, I charge thee, quickly go again,
I bade thee, watch, and lightly bring me word.”
Across the ridge, and paced beside the mere, Counting the dewy pebbles, fixed in thought;
How curiously and strangely chased, he smote His palms together, and he cried aloud:
“And if indeed I cast the brand away,
Should thus be lost for ever from the earth, Which might have pleased the eyes of many men.
What harm, undone? Deep harm to disobey, Seeing obedience is the bond of rule.
An act unprofitable, against himself? The King is sick, and knows not what he does.
Should be to aftertime, but empty breath And rumours of a doubt? But were this kept,
Some one might show it at a joust of arms, Saying, ‘King Arthur’s sword, Excalibur,
Nine years she wrought it, sitting in the deeps Upon the hidden bases of the hills.’
To all the people, winning reverence. But now much honour and much fame were lost.”
And hid Excalibur the second time, And so strode back slow to the wounded King.
“What is it thou hast seen? or what hast heard?”
“I heard the water lapping on the crag, And the long ripple washing in the reeds.”
“Ah, miserable and unkind, untrue, Unknightly, traitor-hearted! Woe is me!
Laid widowed of the power in his eye That bowed the will. I see thee what thou art,
In whom should meet the offices of all, Thou wouldst betray me for the precious hilt;
Valuing the giddy pleasure of the eyes. Yet, for a man may fail in duty twice,
But, if thou spare to fling Excalibur, I will arise and slay thee with my hands.”
And, leaping down the ridges lightly, plunged Among the bulrush beds, and clutched the sword, And strongly wheeled and threw it. The great brand
And flashing round and round, and whirled in an arch, Shot like a streamer of the northern morn,
By night, with noises of the Northern Sea. So flashed and fell the brand Excalibur:
Clothed in white samite, mystic, wonderful, And caught him by the hilt, and brandished him
And lightly went the other to the King.
“Now see I by thine eyes that this is done. Speak out: what is it thou hast heard, or seen?”
“Sir King, I closed mine eyelids, lest the gems Should blind my purpose, for I never saw,
Not though I live three lives of mortal men, So great a miracle as yonder hilt.
But when I looked again, behold an arm, Clothed in white samite, mystic, wonderful,
Three times, and drew him under in the mere.”
“My end draws nigh; ’tis time that I were gone. Make broad thy shoulders to receive my weight,
My wound hath taken cold, and I shall die.”
Slowly, with pain, reclining on his arm, And looking wistfully with wide blue eyes
Remorsefully regarded through his tears, And would have spoken, but he found not words;
O’er both his shoulders drew the languid hands, And rising bore him through the place of tombs.
Like one that feels a nightmare on his bed When all the house is mute. So sighed the King, Muttering and murmuring at his ear, “Quick, quick!
But the other swiftly strode from ridge to ridge, Clothed with his breath, and looking, as he walked,
He heard the deep behind him, and a cry Before. His own thought drove him like a goad.
And barren chasms, and all to left and right The bare black cliff clanged round him, as he based
Sharp-smitten with the dint of armed heels— And on a sudden, lo! the level lake,
Then saw they how there hove a dusky barge,
Beneath them; and descending they were ware That all the decks were dense with stately forms,
Three Queens with crowns of gold: and from them rose A cry that shivered to the tingling stars,
Of lamentation, like a wind that shrills All night in a waste land, where no one comes,
Then murmured Arthur, “Place me in the barge.” So to the barge they came. There those three Queens Put forth their hands, and took the King, and wept.
And fairest, laid his head upon her lap, And loosed the shattered casque, and chafed his hands,
And dropping bitter tears against a brow Striped with dark blood: for all his face was white
Smote by the fresh beam of the springing east; And all his greaves and cuisses dashed with drops
That made his forehead like a rising sun High from the dais-throne—were parched with dust;
Mixed with the knightly growth that fringed his lips. So like a shattered column lay the King;
From spur to plume a star of tournament, Shot through the lists at Camelot, and charged
Then loudly cried the bold Sir Bedivere: “Ah! my Lord Arthur, whither shall I go?
For now I see the true old times are dead, When every morning brought a noble chance,
Such times have been not since the light that led The holy Elders with the gift of myrrh.
Which was an image of the mighty world, And I, the last, go forth companionless,
Among new men, strange faces, other minds.”
“The old order changeth, yielding place to new, And God fulfils himself in many ways,
Comfort thyself: what comfort is in me? I have lived my life, and that which I have done
If thou shouldst never see my face again, Pray for my soul. More things are wrought by prayer Than this world dreams of. Wherefore, let thy voice
For what are men better than sheep or goats That nourish a blind life within the brain,
Both for themselves and those who call them friend? For so the whole round earth is every way
But now farewell. I am going a long way With these thou seest—if indeed I go (For all my mind is clouded with a doubt)—
Where falls not hail, or rain, or any snow, Nor ever wind blows loudly; but it lies
And bowery hollows crowned with summer sea, Where I will heal me of my grievous wound.”
Moved from the brink, like some full-breasted swan That, fluting a wild carol ere her death,
With swarthy webs. Long stood Sir Bedivere Revolving many memories, till the hull
And on the mere the wailing died away.
The stillness of the dead world’s winter dawn Amazed him, and he groaned, “The King is gone.”
“From the great deep to the great deep he goes.”
The last hard footstep of that iron crag; Thence marked the black hull moving yet, and cried, “He passes to be King among the dead,
He comes again; but—if he come no more— O me, be yon dark Queens in yon black boat, Who shrieked and wailed, the three whereat we gazed On that high day, when, clothed with living light,
Of Arthur, who should help him at his need?”
Then from the dawn it seemed there came, but faint
Like the last echo born of a great cry, Sounds, as if some fair city were one voice
Thereat once more he moved about, and clomb
Straining his eyes beneath an arch of hand, Or thought he saw, the speck that bare the King,
Somewhere far off, pass on and on, and go From less to less and vanish into light.
And loyal to thy land, as this to thee— Bear witness, that rememberable day,
Who scarce had plucked his flickering life again From halfway down the shadow of the grave,
And London rolled one tide of joy through all Her trebled millions, and loud leagues of man
The prayer of many a race and creed, and clime— Thunderless lightnings striking under sea
And that true North, whereof we lately heard A strain to shame us “keep you to yourselves;
Is but a burthen: loose the bond, and go.” Is this the tone of empire? here the faith
And meaning, whom the roar of Hougoumont Left mightiest of all peoples under heaven? What shock has fooled her since, that she should speak
The voice of Britain, or a sinking land, Some third-rate isle half-lost among her seas?
Thee and thy Prince! The loyal to their crown Are loyal to their own far sons, who love
For ever-broadening England, and her throne In our vast Orient, and one isle, one isle,
And dreads it we are fallen. —But thou, my Queen, Not for itself, but through thy living love
Sacred, accept this old imperfect tale, New-old, and shadowing Sense at war with Soul,
Rather than that gray king, whose name, a ghost, Streams like a cloud, man-shaped, from mountain peak,
Of Geoffrey’s book, or him of Malleor’s, one Touched by the adulterous finger of a time
And crownings and dethronements: take withal Thy poet’s blessing, and his trust that Heaven
From thine and ours: for some are scared, who mark, Or wisely or unwisely, signs of storm,
And wordy trucklings to the transient hour, And fierce or careless looseners of the faith,
Or Cowardice, the child of lust for gold, Or Labour, with a groan and not a voice,
And that which knows, but careful for itself, And that which knows not, ruling that which knows
Lies beyond sight: yet—if our slowly-grown And crowned Republic’s crowning common-sense,
Are morning shadows huger than the shapes That cast them, not those gloomier which forego The darkness of that battle in the West, Where all of high and holy dies away.
